english: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. Let $p$ be the number of equivalence relations on $A$ having exactly three equivalence classes, each of which contains at least two elements, and let $q$ be the number of equivalence relations on $A$ having exactly two equivalence classes, each of which contains at least two elements. Then the value of $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is ______.
hindi: माना $A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ है। माना $p$, $A$ पर ऐसे तुल्यता संबंधों की संख्या है जिनमें ठीक तीन तुल्यता वर्ग हैं तथा प्रत्येक वर्ग में कम से कम दो अवयव हैं, तथा $q$, $A$ पर ऐसे तुल्यता संबंधों की संख्या है जिनमें ठीक दो तुल्यता वर्ग हैं तथा प्रत्येक वर्ग में कम से कम दो अवयव हैं। तब $\dfrac{p}{q}$ का मान ______ है।
solution: An equivalence relation on $A$ is the same as a partition of $A$ into its classes
$p$: three classes with at least $2$ elements each from $6$ elements must have exactly $2$ each: $p=\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!\,3!}=15$
Two classes: fixed by the class $C$ not containing $6$, any non-empty subset of $\{1,\dots,5\}$: $2^{5}-1=31$
Remove a one-element class: $C$ a singleton ($5$) or $C=\{1,\dots,5\}$, leaving $\{6\}$ alone ($1$): $q=31-6=25$
solution_full: Every equivalence relation on $A$ determines the partition of $A$ into its equivalence classes, and every partition determines exactly one equivalence relation. So $p$ and $q$ count partitions.

Three classes, each with at least $2$ elements, use at least $6$ elements; as $n(A)=6$, every class has exactly $2$ elements. Choose the classes: $\binom62\binom42\binom22=90$ ordered choices, and the $3!$ orders of the same three classes give the same partition: $p=\dfrac{90}{6}=15$.

Two classes: the class $C$ that does not contain $6$ determines the partition (the other class is $A\setminus C$). $C$ can be any non-empty subset of $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, so there are $2^{5}-1=31$ partitions into two classes.

A class with one element occurs when $C$ is a singleton ($5$ ways) or when the class of $6$ is $\{6\}$, i.e. $C=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ ($1$ way). These $6$ cases are excluded: $q=31-6=25$. (Check: $\binom62+\frac12\binom63=15+10=25$ for the types $2+4$ and $3+3$.)
originality_note: New: equivalence relations counted by number of classes under a minimum class size, with the two-class count obtained as 2^5 - 1 minus the singleton cases (way 5: equivalence relations linked with 2^n - 1 selections). Closest known: 'number of equivalence relations on a set with exactly two classes' (Stirling numbers S(n,2) = 2^(n-1) - 1). Different because: the class-size restriction forces the student to remove the singleton cases and to see that three classes of size >= 2 on six elements must be pairs.
